Playground turf for Longwood families

Playground turf in Longwood runs $10–$25 a square foot, typically $12–$19, as of September 2026. Seminole County's own Big Tree Park, a short drive from downtown, already pairs a shaded play structure with a bonded surface, which sets a reasonable bar for what a backyard version should feel like underfoot.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Say you have a swing set going in near the patio

Say you have a 260 sq ft play area planned around a swing set with an 8-foot fall height, in a partly shaded corner of the backyard. At $10–$25 a square foot, that runs $2,600 to $6,500, and at the more typical $12–$19, most quotes land between $3,120 and $4,940, with the shock pad sized to that 8-foot height rather than a standard default. Partial shade from an existing tree keeps the surface noticeably cooler on a summer afternoon than the same layout would run in open sun, though a hose rinse still helps before barefoot play on the hottest days.

What a county park next door gets right

Big Tree Park, home to the cypress once known as The Senator and now to a younger tree called The Phoenix, pairs its play structure with ground-level components and a bonded rubber surface rather than bare mulch. A backyard play area can't use rubber infill across an open lawn, since the state rule limits synthetic infill to the footprint directly under playground equipment, but the same idea, a surface engineered for a fall height rather than left to whatever ground was already there, carries over directly.

The backing still has to drain under a shock pad

Even with a cushioned pad doing most of the impact-absorption work, the turf backing on a Longwood play surface still has to meet the same drainage standard as any other turf product, passing water at over thirty inches an hour. A backing that traps water against the pad below it defeats the purpose of building a well-graded base underneath, since the pad would end up sitting in moisture regardless of how well the rock layer drains. Product selection for a playground job has to account for the pad and the backing working together, not just the pad's rating in isolation.

Sizing the pad to the swing set, not the yard

A shock pad under playground turf gets specified to the equipment's fall height, which means a taller swing set or climbing structure needs a thicker pad than a simple slide does, on the same square footage. Getting that number from the equipment's own manufacturer specification sheet before ordering material avoids the two most common mistakes: a pad too thin for the height it's under, or a pad sized for the tallest piece applied everywhere when only one corner of the layout actually needs it. Fall-height math and infill limits are covered in full in our playground turf guide; the Longwood-specific part is mostly the shade overhead.

Keeping a playground footing off the septic lid

Equipment anchors for a Longwood playground system, and the septic tank's pump-out lid on a property that has one, can't occupy the same footprint, so locating that lid before staking equipment footings and the surrounding base excavation matters here as much as it does for any other part of the yard under the state's access rule. A play area's three-layer stack, rock, pad, turf, makes moving an anchor point after the fact a bigger disruption than adjusting open lawn would be, which is why this gets checked during design rather than once excavation is underway. Keeping the lid a few feet clear of the nearest footing avoids the conflict entirely.

What a swale-adjacent play area risks in a storm

A Longwood play area built too close to a drainage swale, or within ten feet of a pond or canal without a seawall separating the two, runs into the same setback violations a lawn would, but the consequences compound faster here because a shock pad sitting in standing water softens and loses cushioning performance well before the turf itself shows any wear. A base that wasn't graded to keep water moving through and away leaves the pad soaked after every storm, shortening its rated life regardless of how correctly it was matched to the equipment's fall height at installation.

Trimming turf tight to the containment edge

Once the shock pad is bonded in place on a Longwood project, turf goes over it seamed with tape and adhesive the same way it would on a lawn, but the trim line along the containment edge gets more attention here than anywhere else on the job. A wavy or loose cut at that boundary is a common shortcut on a rushed install, and while it doesn't change the pad's rated cushioning, it does leave a lip that can catch a small shoe or let infill wash out during the next storm. This trimming happens only after the pad is fully secured, never before.

Clearing debris before it creates uneven footing

Leaves, acorns, and other debris on a Longwood play surface need regular clearing, more urgently than on a lawn, since anything working down into the infill under active play can create an uneven spot right where a child is running or landing rather than just a cosmetic issue. This is a quick habit during a live oak's seasonal drop, when debris accumulates faster than on an open lawn without canopy overhead. A play area checked weekly during peak leaf-drop stays safer underfoot than one checked only during general yard cleanup.

Building around a canopy families already use for shade

Longwood's tree canopy, the same feature that shapes nearby subdivisions' oak-heavy lots, does double duty for a backyard play area: existing shade keeps a play surface cooler than it would run in full sun, which matters given that unshaded turf commonly reaches 120 to 150°F in direct summer light. Where a play structure sits close enough to a tree to raise a drip-line question, the same certified-arborist rule that applies to a lawn conversion applies here too.

Questions people ask

Can rubber infill go under a Longwood backyard play structure?

Yes, but only inside the footprint of the equipment itself. The state's rule reserves rubber and other synthetic infill for that specific area; the rest of the yard still uses silica sand, coated sand or zeolite.

Does playground turf near Big Tree Park's example need a specific pad thickness?

There's no county standard for a backyard project; the pad thickness follows the equipment manufacturer's stated fall height, which varies by structure rather than by location in Longwood.
